notes.short: “Useless”: a mild word for a real wrong
notes.about: Paul says Onesimus was formerly useless to Philemon. The word is gentle, for he had done his master real wrong (see verse 18). Paul names the fault softly and turns at once to the change: now he is useful to Philemon and to Paul.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: the real harm Onesimus had done his master, put in the mildest word

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis, since Onesimus had done real injury. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Onesimus was not only unprofitable but positively injurious, having wronged his master, and that Paul uses a mild expression. Benson says Paul gives the fault the softest name possible and passes at once to the happy change in him.
notes.limit: The note does not say what the wrong was: Paul says only “if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything” (verse 18).

cites.quote: “Which in time past was to thee unprofitable.” This is a Meiosis, for Onesimus was guilty of injury.
